header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, PESHAWAR
Present: Mr. Tariq Iqbal Khattak, Advocate for
body: Date of Announcement: 16.11.2026 JJUUDDGGMMEENNTT MMUUHHAAMMMMAADD IIJJAAZZ KKHHAANN,, JJ..-- Through this petition, the petitioner has challenged the orders of the learned trial court / Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Kohat dated 08.04.2026 and 20.04.2026, whereby the learned trial Court recalled the exemption from personal appearance previously granted to the petitioner upon completion of the prosecution evidence vide the impugned former order dated 08.04.2026, and subsequently, dismissed the petitioner's application for grant of exemption from personal appearance and he was declared absconder with the initiation of proceedings under section 514 Cr.P.C against his sureties with the direction to Muharrir to prepare a separate file for proceedings under section 512 Cr.P.C and the case was consigned to the record room vide the impugned latter order dated 20.04.2026.

2. Precisely, the facts leading to the filing of this petition are that the present petitioner is facing trial in case FIR No. 563 dated 30.09.2022 under Section 11-B of The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 2019 read with Section 15- AA registered at Police Station Cantt, Kohat, and when he was summoned by the learned trial court, he submitted an application for exemption of his personal appearance through his duly nominated counsel on the ground that he is earning his livelihood abroad, which application, after a due contest, was allowed by the learned trial court vide order dated 11.05.2024, whereby the petitioner was exempted from his personal appearance before the trial court till further order and it was also directed that he is to be represented by a duly nominated counsel. Thereafter, the trial of the petitioner commenced in which his counsel was regularly representing him, and ultimately when the evidence of the persecution was completed on 08.04.2026, the learned trial court on the same day recalled the exemption of the petitioner and the learned counsel representing the petitioner was directed to ensure the attendance of the petitioner for recording of his statement. Simultaneously, notices were also issued to his sureties, however, on the following two adjourned dates i.e. 15.04.2026 and 20.04.2026, the petitioner did not appear, and then thereafter, he was declared absconder with the initiation of proceedings under section 514 Cr.P.C against his sureties with the direction to Muharrir to prepare a separate file for proceedings under section 512 Cr.P.C and the case was consigned to the record room vide impugned order dated 20.04.2026, which order has now been challenged by the petitioner before this court.

3. Detailed arguments of the learned counsel for the petitioner as well as learned AAG representing the State were heard. During the course of arguments, the only question which arises in this case is that when an accused has been granted exemption by the court from personal appearance, then whether his statement under section 342 Cr.P.C could be recorded in his absence, and as to whether in the course of his aforesaid statement such an accused could be represented by his duly nominated pleader / counsel or not?

4. In order to answer the aforesaid question, it would be appropriate to first highlight the relevant facts leading to the filing of this petition, which are to the effect that initially when the present petitioner was charged in the instant FIR, he was released on bail, and when the investigation was completed and challan was put in court, the Learned Special Court issued summon to the present petitioner for his attendance, however, since he was already abroad, therefore, instead of personal appearance, he appointed his counsel, and who on his behalf put appearance before the learned Trial Court and submitted an application for grant of exemption from personal appearance of the petitioner, which was duly noticed to the State, and after hearing the learned counsel for the petitioner and worthy Prosecutor, the learned Trial Court exempted the present petitioner from his personal appearance till further order, and was allowed to be represented by his duly nominated counsel and thereafter compliance of section 265-C Cr.P.C was also made through his counsel vide order dated 11.05.2024. Similarly, the charge was also framed in his absence, and the evidence of the prosecution was also recorded, and the present petitioner was allowed to be represented by his counsel, however, when the evidence of prosecution was closed, thereafter, the exemption granted to the present petitioner was recalled, vide one of the impugned order dated 08.04.2026 and the learned counsel representing the petitioner was strictly directed to ensure the attendance of the petitioner for recording his statement under section 342 Cr.P.C and the case was adjourned to 20.04.2026 and who vide the second impugned order and judgment dated 20.04.2026, issued Non-bailable warrant of arrest (NBW) against the present petitioner, and his sureties which orders have now been challenged by the petitioner before this Court through the instant petition.

5. Keeping insight the aforesaid admitted fact that right from the start of the trial of the petitioner i.e. supply of documents (Section 265-C Cr.P.C) and framing of charge (Section 265-D Cr.P.C) till the conclusion of the prosecution evidence, the petitioner has been represented by his counsel. There is no cavil with the proposition that the presence of an accused is essential at different stages of the trial, as per the mandate of various provisions of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C”) and in this regard, Chapter XXII-A of Cr.P.C, which deals with the trial of an accused by the Court of Sessions is relevant, and as per section 265-C Cr.P.C, the documents mentioned thereunder are to be supplied free of cost to the accused, whereas, as per Section 265-D Cr.P.C read with Section 265-E Cr.P.C, if on the basis of police report and other documents filed by the prosecution, the trial court is of the opinion that there are sufficient material to proceed with the trial of the accused, then it shall frame the charge in writing against the accused, and which is to be read and explained to the accused and then the accused shall be asked, whether he is guilty, or he has any Section 265-C. Supply of statements and documents to the accused.—(1) In all cases instituted upon police report, copies of the following documents shall be supplied free of cost to the accused not later than seven days before the commencement of the trial, namely:— (a) the first information report;
(b) the police report;

(c) the statements of all witnesses recorded under sections 161 and 164; and (d) the inspection note recorded by an investigating officer on his first visit to the place of occurrence and the note recorded by him on recoveries made, if any: Provided that, if any part of a statement recorded under section 161 or section 164 is such that its disclosure to the accused would be inexpedient in the public interest, such part of the statement shall be excluded from the copy of the statement furnished to the accused. (2) In all cases instituted upon a complaint in writing— (a) the complainant shall— (i) state in the petition of complaint the substance of the accusation, the names of his witnesses and the gist of the evidence which he is likely to adduce at the trial; and (ii) within three days of the order of the Court under section 204 for issue of process to the accused, file in the Court for supply to the accused as many copies of the complaint and any other document which he has filed with his complaint as the number of the accused; (b) copies of the complaint and any other documents which the complainant has filed therewith and the statements under section 200 or section 202 shall be supplied free of cost to the accused not later than seven days before the commencement of the trial. Section 265-D, Cr.P.C. — When charge is to be framed. If, after perusing the police report or, as the case may be, the complaint, and all other documents and statements filed by the prosecution, the Court is of opinion that there is ground for proceeding with the trial of the accused it shall frame in writing a charge against the accused. Section 265-E Cr.P.C. — Plea (1) The charge shall be read and explained to the accused, and he shall be asked whether he is guilty or has any defence to make. (2) If the accused pleads guilty, the Court shall record the plea, and may in its discretion convict him thereon.

defence to make. Similarly, after the framing of charge, as per mandate of section 353 Cr.P.C, the evidence of the prosecution shall be taken in the presence of the accused, or when his personal attendance is dispensed with, then in presence of his pleader, and after the closure of the evidence, the statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C is to be recorded, which is having the object and purpose to enable the accused to explain all those circumstances, which have been brought by the prosecution in evidence against him, whereas section Cr.P.C lays down the mode and manner, in which the aforesaid statement of accused is to be recorded, which mandates that the reply of an accused shall be recorded in full and in the language, in which accused is being examined, whereas Section 353, Cr.P.C. — Evidence to be taken in presence of accused..— Except as otherwise expressly provided, all evidence taken under Chapters XX, XXI, XXII and XXII-A shall be taken in the presence of the accused, or, when his personal attendance is dispensed with, in presence of his pleader Section 364, Cr.P.C. — Examination of accused how recorded (1) Whenever the accused is examined by any Magistrate, or by any Court other than a High Court, the whole of such examination, including every question put to him and every answer given by him, shall be recorded in full, in the language in which he is examined, or, if that is not practicable, in the language of the Court or in English: and such record shall be shown or read to him, or, if he does not understand the language in which it is written, shall be interpreted to him in a language which he understands, and he shall be at liberty to explain or add to his answers.

(2) When the whole is made conformable to what he declares is the truth, the record shall be signed by the accused and the Magistrate or Judge of such Court, and such Magistrate or Judge shall certify under his own hand that the examination was taken in his presence and hearing and that the record contains a full and true account of the statement made by the accused.

(3) In cases in which the examination of the accused is not recorded by the Magistrate or Judge himself, he shall be bound, as the examination proceeds, to make a memorandum thereof in the language of the Court, or in English, if he is sufficiently acquainted with the latter language; and such memorandum shall be written and signed by the Magistrate or Judge with his own hand, and shall be annexed to the record. If the Magistrate or Judge is unable to make a memorandum as above required, he shall record the reason of such inability.
(4) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to apply to the examination of an accused person under section 263.

subsection (2) of section 364 Cr.P.C, requires that such statement is to be signed by the accused and a declaration and certificate is to be made / issued by the Judge in his own handwriting to the effect that the aforesaid examination of the accused was taken in his presence and hearing and that it contains a full and true account of the statement made by the accused.

6. The combined perusal of the aforesaid various provisions of the Cr.P.C would show that as a general rule, the presence of the accused, at the every stage of the trial, is essential, however, the law simultaneously provides that an accused person could be dispensed with from his personal appearance by the Judge, who is conducting trial of the accused, and, in this regard, section 205 Cr.P.C provides that if, the Magistrate, at the time of issuance of summon, sees some reasons that there are certain circumstances, which require that the personal attendance of the accused be dispensed with, and he may be allowed to appear by his Section 205. Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused. (1)Whenever a Magistrate issues a summons, he may, if he sees reason so to do, dispense with the personal attendance of the accused, and permit him to appear by his pleader. (2) But the Magistrate inquiring into or trying the case may, in his discretion, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of the accused, and, if necessary, enforce such attendance in manner hereinbefore provided. Pleader, whereas, section 540-A Cr.P.C stipulates that if, during pendency of the trial, the Judge is satisfied for reasons to be recorded that an accused is incapable of remaining before the court, and if such accused is represented by a Pleader, then, he may in its discretion dispense with his personal attendance and proceed with the trial in his absence, and such Judge may at any subsequent stage of the proceedings direct the personal attendance of such an accused. In the given facts and circumstances, what could be gathered from the aforesaid different provisions of law is that, the personal attendance of an accused is the foundation for conducting a fair trial, however, simultaneously the court has a power to dispense with the personal attendance of an accused and to proceed with the trial by allowing such accused to be represented by a duly appointed counsel, and thus, the, question as was framed in the preceding para can further be bifurcated into two questions:- Section 540-A. Provision for inquiries and trial being held in the absence of accused in certain cases.(1) At any stage of an inquiry or trial under this Code, where two or more accused are before the Court, if the Judge or Magistrate is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, that any one or more of such accused is or are incapable of remaining before the Court, he may, if such accused is represented by a pleader, dispense with his attendance and proceed with such inquiry or trial in his absence, and may, at any subsequent stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of such accused. (2) If the accused in any such case is not represented by a pleader, or if the Judge or Magistrate considers his personal attendance necessary, he may, if he thinks fit, and for reasons to be recorded by him, either adjourn such inquiry or trial, or order that the case of such accused be taken up or tried separately. i. Whether a statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C could be recorded in a case where personal attendance of such an accused has lawfully been exempted by the court?; and ii. Whether a statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C could be recorded in his absence where the accused has deliberately absented/absconded or residing abroad, without obtaining any proper exemption?

7. In order to answer the aforesaid questions, now, this court would again revert to section 205 and Section 540-A Cr.P.C, which reads as under:- Section 205. Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused. (1)
Whenever a Magistrate issues a summons, he may, if he sees reason so to do, dispense with the personal attendance of the accused, and permit him to appear by his pleader.

(2) But the Magistrate inquiring into or trying the case may, in his discretion, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of the accused, and, if necessary, enforce such attendance in manner hereinbefore provided.

Section 540-A. Provision for inquiries and trial being held in the absence of accused in certain cases.(1) At any stage of an inquiry or trial under this Code, where two or more accused are before the Court, if the Judge or Magistrate is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, that any one or more of such accused is or are incapable of remaining before the Court, he may, if such accused is represented by a pleader, dispense with his attendance and proceed with such inquiry or trial in his absence, and may, at any subsequent stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of such accused.

(2) If the accused in any such case is not represented by a pleader, or if the Judge or Magistrate considers his personal attendance necessary, he may, if he thinks fit, and for reasons to be recorded by him, either adjourn such inquiry or trial, or order that the case of such accused be taken up or tried separately. (Underline is for emphasis)

The plain reading of Section 205 Cr.P.C would unmistakenly show that if the Magistrate, at the time of issuance of a summon, is of the opinion to dispense with the personal attendance of the accused, then it may pass such an order, and could permit such an accused to appear by his Pleader. Similarly, Section 540-A Cr.P.C also confers such power on the trial Judge that where it is of the opinion that the accused has rendered incapable for remaining before such court, then he may, if such an accused, is represented by a pleader dispense with his attendance, and proceed with the trial in his absence, and may require the attendance of such accused, subsequently if it so considered appropriate. Both these provisions of law would manifestly show that the legislature were very clear in their intention that the trial of an accused person could be conducted in his absence right from the very inception, i.e. supply of documents under section 265-C Cr.P.C till its conclusion. Had the legislature intended to ensure the presence of an accused at the time of recording a statement under section 342 Cr.P.C, then, they could have specifically legislated and enacted upon such a provision-cum-a condition thereunder, and thus, absence of any such requirement of law rendered it to leave to the discretion of the court, who has granted exemption to an accused person, and as as stated hereinabove that in the present case, the petitioner has never ever appeared before the trial court at any stage of his trial and when the summon was issued then soon thereafter, the petitioner put his appearance through his counsel, and even formalities of supply of documents as required under section 265-C Cr.P.C and framing of charge under Section 265-D were carried out in his absence, therefore, it can safely be concluded that the trial court has exercised its discretion in favour of the present petitioner that he is to be represented by a duly appointed counsel, therefore, the trial court should have also been recorded the statement of the petitioner through his counsel, as there is no legal bar to record the same through his counsel. The question as to whether the statement of an accused could be recorded under section 342 Cr.P.C in his absence has remained a favorite subject of the Superior Judiciary, and in this regard, it would be relevant to make reference to a mother judgment rendered by the Lahore High Court in a case wherein it recognizes that a pleader may be examined under Section 342 Cr.P.C on behalf of the accused who has already been exempted from appearance. It has further been held that the provisions of section 342 Cr.P.C are controlled by those of the section 205 Cr.P.C and the latter one (Section 205 Cr.P.C) further stipulates that throughout the trial the court need not insist upon the personal appearance of the accused unless for some recorded reason it thinks otherwise and it has been concluded that the examination of the pleaders on behalf of the accused under section 342 Cr.P.C could neither be termed as an illegality or even an irregularity in the trial. Similarly, this court in a case has ruled that the accused-petitioner was serving in Libya as Professor and was also suffering from heart disease and he was refused exemption by the trial court, therefore, this court held that the said accused is entitled for exemption under Section 540-A Cr.P.C and as such a charge against the said accused could be framed and even the statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C could be The Crown .vs. Jehan Dad and others, PLD 1954 Lahore 107 (DB) Dr. Ali Yahyah .vs. the State, 1989 P Cr.LJ 1652 recorded through his counsel. Similarly, in another case , wherein it was held that section 342, Cr.P.C. must be read as subject to the provisions of section 205 and that the trial Magistrate is not bound to question the accused person under section 342, Cr.P.C., if the latter had been exempted from personal appearance and appears by a pleader. A similar view prevailed with a Single Judge of the Rangoon High Court in a case wherein it has been held that there is also an earlier D.A. judgment of Bombay High Court reported as Dorabshah Bomanji Dubash v. Emperor, AIR 1926 Bom. 218, wherein it was ruled that the Court can act upon the plea given by the pleader of an accused whose attendance has been excused under section 342, Cr.P.C. That was a case tried under the summons case procedure and the relevant sections were sections 242 and 243, Cr.P.C., but the analogy seems to be apt. In another Single Bench judgment of the Allahabad High Court reported as Bechu Chaube v. King Emperor, AIR 1923 AII. 81, it was held that failure to apply the provisions of section 342, Cr.P.C. constitutes an error and not an irregularity and if does Emperor v. Jaffar Cassum Moosa, AIR 1934 Bom. 212 Maung Po Nyein v. Haka Singh, AIR 1927 Rang.73 not prejudice the accused, may be condoned under the provisions of section 537, Cr.P.C., provided that it concerned matter of procedure rather than the mode of trial. The opinion was expressed in Emperor v. Mst. Jamal Khatun, 14 Cr. LJ 272 (DB), that the appearance by a pleader after an order is passed under section 205, Cr.P.C., involved the performance by the pleader of all acts which devolved upon the accused in the course of the trial. The preponderance of authority, therefore, seems to be in favour of the proposition that the provisions of section 342, Cr.P.C., are controlled by those of section 205 of the Code.

8. In the view of the aforesaid mandate of law, when once this court has concluded that even the statement of an accused under Section 342 Cr.P.C could be recorded in his absence and he could be duly represented by a counsel, then the next question is that as to whether the judgment could be announced / delivered in the absence of the accused or not? In this regard, subsection (2) & (3) of section 366 Cr.P.C being relevant is reproduced below:- Section 366. Mode of delivering judgment.—(1) …………………………………… (2) The accused shall, if in custody, be brought up, or, if not in custody, be required by the Court to attend, to hear judgment delivered, except where his personal attendance during the trial has been dispensed with and the sentence is one of fine only or he is acquitted, in either of which cases it may be delivered in the presence of his pleader.

(3) No judgment delivered by any Criminal Court shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the absence of any party or his pleader on the day or from the place notified for the delivery thereof, or of any omission to serve, or defect in serving, on the parties or their pleaders, or any of them, the notice of such day and place.

The plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law laid down the mode and manner in which a judgment has to be delivered and as such it mandates that if the accused is in custody then he is to be brought before the court, however, if he is not in the custody then the court may require the attendance of an accused to hear the judgment except where his personal attendance during the trial has been dispensed with, and if the sentence is one of fine only or he is acquitted, such judgment could be delivered in the presence of his pleader. The aforesaid provision draws a distinction that where the judgment is containing fine only or if the trial court is going to acquit an accused then such acquittal could be ordered in presence of his pleader, however, correspondingly it speaks that if the trial court is going to convict an accused then presence of an accused would be required, however, if such condition is read conjointly with subsection (3) ibid, then even an order of conviction recorded in absence of an accused could not be termed as invalid for the only reasons that it was delivered in the absence of an accused person, therefore, even a conviction order could be delivered in the absence of an accused person, nevertheless such order is to be implemented in its letter and spirit whenever the convict accused person is arrested and brought before the Court. In the ibid judgment of The Crown .vs. Jehan Dad, it has also been held that considering the language of section 205 of the Code, it is plain that throughout the trial, the Court need not insist upon the personal appearance of the accused unless for some reason it thinks otherwise. Reference in this connection may also usefully be made to the provisions of subsection (2) of section 366 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which enacts that where the personal appearance of the accused had been dispensed with, during the trial and the sentence is one of the fine only or he is acquitted, the judgment may be delivered in the presence of the pleader representing him. The conclusion is also strengthened by reference to the provisions of section 540-A Cr.P.C. We hold, therefore, that there has been no illegality or even irregularity in the trial consequent on the pleader being examined on behalf of the women accused in this case under section 342, Cr.P.C. The contention raised on behalf of the Crown must be repelled as unsound.

9. In view of the above, it is held and concluded as under:- I. That the presence of an accused before the trial court is mandatory, however, equally the trial Judge has the lawful authority to dispense with the personal attendance of the accused and to allow him to be represented by his pleader and to proceed with the trial;

II. That as a general rule, the statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C is to be recorded in presence of accused, however, such statement could validly be recorded in his absence and the same could validly be recorded through his pleader, if he has lawfully been exempted from personal appearance by the trial Judge; and III. The statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C could not be recorded in his absence if he has deliberately absented himself or has opted to abscond or is residing abroad without obtaining an exemption from his personal appearance.

10. In view of the above discussion and exposition of law on the subject, this criminal revision petition is allowed, consequently, the impugned orders and judgment dated 08.04.2026 and 20.04.2026 of the learned trial court are set aside and as a result thereof, the learned trial is directed to restore the trial of the petitioner and to record the statement of the accused-petitioner under Section 342 Cr.P.C through his pleader and shall thereafter deliver a judgment on its own merits and in accordance with law. Order accordingly.
